articleMarkdown:
# Studying Kǎn (Repeated Water): responding step by step when difficulties keep returning

When difficulties recur, start with facts you can verify and look for a way forward through small steps available now.

When the same problem keeps returning, it can feel as though there are only two choices: charge straight through or conclude that nothing can be done. Kǎn describes repeated danger through pits and flowing water, while also making room for modest gains and plain communication at different stages. Studying it may help reduce confusion, but a hexagram cannot assess real-world danger or replace necessary protection and help.

## Identity and line order

Kǎn is hexagram 29 in the traditional King Wen sequence, with symbol ䷜. The lower trigram is Kǎn ☵ and the upper trigram is Kǎn ☵; their traditional images are water and water, respectively. Count the lines from the bottom: 初六、九二、六三、六四、九五、上六. A solid line is yang and a broken line is yin. Nine and six in the line labels designate yang and yin; they are not additional line numbers.

```text
━━━━ ━━━━  上六
━━━━━━━━━  九五
━━━━ ━━━━  六四
━━━━ ━━━━  六三
━━━━━━━━━  九二
━━━━ ━━━━  初六
```

## Hexagram statement

習坎：有孚，維心亨，行有尚。

Original editorial rendering; not a quotation from Legge: Repeated danger: there is sincerity; the heart finds a way through, and action has worth.

Here xí suggests repetition or doubling: Kǎn appears both below and above. Legge reads Kǎn as a pit, a dangerous hollow, or a ravine through which water flows, and connects having sincerity with a steady inner foundation.

For a modern reflection, first distinguish what is repeating: have the conditions stayed the same, has the approach stayed the same, or is the information still unclear? Making the problem specific creates room for adjustment. Feeling afraid is not a character flaw, and an unfavorable divinatory statement cannot establish that a situation is hopeless.

References: [zhouyi-29](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/坎&oldid=10646381), [legge1882-29](https://tianmu.org/good-work-library/confucian/general-texts/the-i-ching-james-legge)

## Interpretations in the Ten Wings

The Commentary on the Judgment and the Commentary on the Images belong to the commentarial collection known as the Yìzhuàn, usually called the Ten Wings. Below, these commentaries are kept separate from the hexagram and line statements, followed by modern learning applications.

The Commentary on the Judgment explains repeated Kǎn as danger upon danger. The Commentary on the Images describes water arriving again and again, and speaks of constancy in conduct and practice in teaching. These commentaries connect sustained engagement with practice.

Today, this may mean preparing clear checking procedures, recording what has worked, and verifying things with trustworthy people. Practice should improve practical judgment, not require someone to keep proving their courage in genuine danger.

References: [zhouyi-29](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/坎&oldid=10646381), [hon-sep](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/chinese-change/)

## The six lines, from bottom to top

### 初六 · Avoid making the difficulty deeper

習坎，入于坎窞，凶。

Original editorial rendering; not a quotation from Legge: Repeated danger: entering a pit within the pit. Misfortune.

The first line pictures someone already amid repeated danger entering another hollow. Legge emphasizes that movement can deepen the predicament; moving does not always provide an escape.

If an approach keeps adding costs, stop repeating it for a while and identify the missing information. This does not judge the reader's fate or blame difficulties on a lack of personal strength.

References: [zhouyi-29](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/坎&oldid=10646381), [legge1882-29](https://tianmu.org/good-work-library/confucian/general-texts/the-i-ching-james-legge)

### 九二 · First secure a little verifiable progress

坎有險，求小得。

Original editorial rendering; not a quotation from Legge: There is danger in the pit; seek a small gain.

The text does not demand an immediate escape from danger; it calls for a small gain. Legge likewise distinguishes partial relief from completely overcoming the difficulty.

With a complex task, first resolve one obstacle you can check, such as confirming the right contact or supplying a missing document. A small advance should not be inflated into a claim that everything is solved, but it can genuinely support the next step.

References: [zhouyi-29](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/坎&oldid=10646381), [legge1882-29](https://tianmu.org/good-work-library/confucian/general-texts/the-i-ching-james-legge)

### 六三 · Reassess when both advance and retreat are blocked

來之坎坎，險且枕，入于坎窞，勿用。

Original editorial rendering; not a quotation from Legge: Coming and going, pit after pit; danger and an uneasy resting place. Entering the pit within the pit: do not proceed.

When danger meets movement in either direction, action alone no longer guarantees improvement. Legge retains the warning against continuing the existing course at this point.

If several options all rest on the same mistaken assumption, examine that assumption rather than hastily switching between them. A pause should clarify the problem, not mean abandoning action forever.

References: [zhouyi-29](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/坎&oldid=10646381), [legge1882-29](https://tianmu.org/good-work-library/confucian/general-texts/the-i-ching-james-legge)

### 六四 · Communication can be simple and practical

樽酒簋貳，用缶，納約自牖，終无咎。

Original editorial rendering; not a quotation from Legge: A vessel of wine and two food bowls, using earthenware; a simple offering is brought through the window. In the end, no blame.

Wine, food vessels, and an earthenware jar form a modest offering; yǒu means a window. Legge develops the line through unostentatious sincerity and an approach the other person can understand.

When you need help, clearly describing the facts, what you have already tried, and the specific question may work better than an elaborate appeal. Sincere communication still requires choosing an appropriate person; it does not mean entrusting private information or confidence to anyone at all.

References: [zhouyi-29](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/坎&oldid=10646381), [legge1882-29](https://tianmu.org/good-work-library/confucian/general-texts/the-i-ching-james-legge)

### 九五 · Notice how conditions gradually open up

坎不盈，禔既平，无咎。

Original editorial rendering; not a quotation from Legge: The pit is not overflowing; it has reached a level state. No blame.

Legge reads this line as water not yet overflowing and a situation moving toward clearance and level ground. The image concerns changes within danger, not a guaranteed outcome for every reader.

When a problem eases, check which conditions have actually changed. Record what worked and identify what remains unresolved, rather than letting relief bring verification to an end.

References: [zhouyi-29](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/坎&oldid=10646381), [legge1882-29](https://tianmu.org/good-work-library/confucian/general-texts/the-i-ching-james-legge)

### 上六 · Serious constraints need to be recognized

係用徽纆，寘于叢棘，三歲不得，凶。

Original editorial rendering; not a quotation from Legge: Bound with cords and placed among thorns; for three years, no release. Misfortune.

Cords and thickets of thorns portray deep confinement. Legge places the image in a setting of imprisonment while acknowledging that its particular historical reference is unclear.

This passage does not predict three years of hardship. If you are being constrained or harmed in real life, or cannot resolve a persistent problem, seek appropriate support. The ancient text is not grounds for concluding that endurance is your only option or that nobody can help.

References: [zhouyi-29](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/坎&oldid=10646381), [legge1882-29](https://tianmu.org/good-work-library/confucian/general-texts/the-i-ching-james-legge)

## Handling a repeatedly stalled document submission

Original modern scenario

An organizer has her event documents returned several times. At first, she simply keeps changing the formatting. Later, she lists all the feedback and discovers that the same confirmation information has been missing each time. She stops repeatedly uploading the documents and contacts someone who can explain the requirements.

She supplies that item first, then checks the remaining material step by step. Resolving one issue does not lead her to declare the entire process complete. If the information she receives still conflicts, she asks for further clarification.

The lesson drawn from Kǎn here is to reduce repetition without a sound basis and find a small but real opening. It does not guarantee a waiting period or an approval result.

## Misreadings to avoid

- Kǎn does not mean being born unlucky, and cannot assess actual accident, health, or financial risks. Unfavorable statements belong in the context of ancient divinatory language.

- Images of water and pits do not provide water-safety or rescue instructions. Actual danger requires appropriate practical protection and assistance.

## Three practices

1. Write down a problem that has recently recurred and identify what has truly been the same each time.

2. Find one small step whose result you can verify, without requiring it to solve everything at once.

3. Record which condition needs to change before continuing, so that repetition does not keep increasing the strain.

## Related hexagram

### Lí — The Clinging Fire (hexagram-30)

Kǎn considers responding amid danger; Lí can extend the inquiry to the conditions that support clear understanding. Steady action and clear knowledge both matter in difficulty; courage or imagination alone is not enough.

## A closing question

While reading Kǎn, ask: is there a small, still-unchecked fact that could spare me from repeating the same difficulty?

## Textual note

The fourth line follows the complete variant explicitly listed in the base edition: “樽酒簋貳，用缶，納約自牖”. The fifth line retains “禔” from the main text.
